title: A 99-Year-Old Grandma Walked to Make Freedom Day a Real Holiday!
summary: Imagine waiting more than two years to hear the best news ever! That's what happened to 250,000 enslaved people in Texas. In 1863, President Lincoln said they were free. But plantation owners hid the truth. Finally, on June 19, 1865, Union soldiers arrived in Galveston and shouted, "You're free!" The joy exploded into dancing, prayers, and big cookouts. That celebration became Juneteenth. But for a long time, it wasn't an official holiday everywhere. That bugged Opal Lee, a grandma from Texas. In 2016, when she was 89, she started walking. She walked 2.5 miles in cities all the way from Fort Worth to Washington, DC. Why 2.5 miles? It stood for the 2.5 years people waited to learn they were free. Her feet and her heart made a difference. In 2021, President Biden signed a law making Juneteenth a federal holiday. Now 99, Opal says, "Juneteenth is not a Black thing, and it's not a Texas thing. We all bleed red blood." So this June 19, grab some barbecue and remember: freedom is for everyone!
why_it_matters: Opal Lee's story shows that one person, no matter how old, can change the country's calendar so that everyone remembers how important freedom is.

background_read: The Emancipation Proclamation by President Abraham Lincoln in 1863 declared freedom for enslaved people in Confederate states, but plantation owners often hid the news to keep their workers.

Opal Lee (a retired teacher and activist from Fort Worth, Texas, sometimes called the 'Grandmother of Juneteenth') began her walking campaign at age 89 to persuade the whole country to honor this important day.
Galveston, a city on the Texas coast, is where Union soldiers finally arrived in 1865 to enforce the proclamation, sparking celebrations that became Juneteenth.
Article_Structure: WHO: Opal Lee, a determined 99-year-old grandma from Texas.
WHAT: She walked 2.5 miles in cities across the country to push for Juneteenth to become a national holiday.
WHERE: From Fort Worth, Texas all the way to Washington, DC.
WHY: Because the 2.5 years enslaved people waited for freedom deserved to be remembered by everyone as a celebration of freedom for all.

perspectives.description: They believe Juneteenth should be a national holiday so all Americans can learn about the end of slavery and celebrate freedom together. The 2.5-mile walks turned her personal mission into a movement.

For many Black Texans, Juneteenth was already a cherished local tradition. Some worried that making it a federal holiday might water down its meaning, but Opal Lee sees the national recognition as a way to share joy and history with everyone.
